open-question.question: Project file paths are written unquoted on the commit tool's command line (`<PATHS>` in the commit procedure, the recorded paths in the inline completion call), so a path holding a space or a shell-active character breaks the call, while the completion agent's path file, read line-exact, is unaffected. How do such paths reach the commit tool: quoted under a rule stated where the command is shown, through the path-file form for every caller, or as they do now?

recommendation.option: Path list on stdin at completion call

open-question.recommendation: Arbitrary project paths reach a command line only at the inline completion call, and a line-exact heredoc there gives it the same no-escaping path form the agent's path file already has, at the cost of one small tested addition to the commit tool.

alternative.id: Path list on stdin at completion call

open-question.alternative: The commit tool's path-file reader gains `-` for standard input, and only the inline completion call passes its recorded paths and `<MISSION_DIR>/TASKS_TODO.md` as `--path-file -` fed by a quoted heredoc, one path per line. The commit procedure's command stays unquoted, with the same recorded reason that its paths are plugin-named. The change is pinned by commit-tool tests and the completion call's fixed-call test. Arbitrary paths are fully protected at the one site they occur, with no escaping rule for the runner. The commit procedure and the many skills that follow it stay untouched. A tool change serves a single caller. Two path-passing forms then sit beside the orchestrator's file form. The procedure keeps its gap, which is safe only on the Mission path characters question's terms. A body on standard input is ruled out for this call (Commit body quoting question).

Both command lines take quoted paths under one stated rule. The commit procedure's command is shown as `--remove "<REMOVAL>" -- "<PATHS>"`, with the sentence beside it saying every path is written in its own double quotes with any `"`, `$`, backtick, or `\` escaped by a backslash. That is the wording the answer sweep's batched call and `submit-task`'s call already state. The inline completion call's fence shows `"<recorded path 1>" "<recorded path 2>"` under the same rule. The commit tool and the orchestrator's path-file call stay unchanged. The change is pinned by extending the inline completion call's fixed-call test with a recorded path holding a space and a `$`, plus a new test that extracts the procedure's command. Every character is closed at both sites through the one quoting rule the plugin already states elsewhere. The tool is not changed, and each command keeps the shape runners already know. Correctness still depends on the runner escaping every path. A missed `$` or backtick inside double quotes still expands without any error. No test extracts the procedure's command yet, so one must be added. Whether the `<MISSION_DIR>` part of each path is quoted the same way depends on the Mission path characters question.

Only the inline completion call's recorded paths are quoted, each in its own double quotes under the sweep's and `submit-task`'s backslash-escaping rule, stated beside that fence. The change is pinned by extending its fixed-call test with a spaced and a `$`-holding path. The commit procedure's command stays unquoted. CLAUDE.md records the reason that its PATHS and REMOVALS are only plugin-named files: the context file, the principle store, and mission files and directories, never an arbitrary project path. It is the smallest change that closes the one site where arbitrary project paths reach the command line. No new procedure test and no tool change are needed. The procedure keeps the gap, so a later caller that passes a project path through it inherits the breakage. The procedure is safe only if mission paths can never hold such characters, which the Mission path characters question decides.

The commit tool's line-exact path-file reader gains `-` as a value meaning standard input. Both the commit procedure's command and the inline completion call then pass PATHS as `--path-file -` fed by a quoted heredoc, one path per line, with no quoting or escaping. `--remove` stays an argument as it is now. The orchestrator's `--path-file "<scratch dir>/paths.txt"` call is unchanged. The change is pinned by new commit-tool tests and the extended fixed-call tests. Nothing depends on the runner escaping anything. Any character but a newline reaches git as written, through the same line-exact read the completion agent's path file already relies on. Every caller then passes paths in one form. The tool's contract changes, and every committing skill's shown command takes a new form. Standard input is used up by the path list, so the procedure's body cannot also arrive that way, which the Commit body quoting question owns. The heredoc delimiter rule (Heredoc delimiter clause question) now matters for paths too. The `--remove` arguments stay unprotected.

alternative.id: Temp path file at completion call

open-question.alternative: The inline completion call writes its recorded paths and `<MISSION_DIR>/TASKS_TODO.md` from a quoted heredoc into a file made by `mktemp`, one path per line, and passes it as `--path-file`. This is exactly the form the orchestrator's commit-from-file call already uses, and the commit tool is unchanged. The commit procedure's command stays unquoted, with the recorded reason that its paths are plugin-named. The change is pinned by the completion call's fixed-call test. It reuses the already tested line-exact path-file read with no tool change and no escaping rule, so a recorded path of any shape reaches git as written. Every inline completion leaves a temp file behind, since the plugin keeps delete commands out of runner prose. The call gains a held file path and one more step to get right. The procedure's gap remains, which is safe only on the Mission path characters question's terms.

Both command lines stay as they are, with paths unquoted. CLAUDE.md records the case as accepted with its reason. No tracked path in this repository holds a space or a shell-active character. Most breakages are loud: a split path makes `git add` fail on a pathspec after the retry window, zsh stops on an unmatched glob, and a parenthesis is a syntax error. In each of those cases nothing is committed and the tree stays resumable. No test is added, since no tool or fixed call changes. It costs nothing and changes no contract, test, or command. The paths this plugin's own projects record show no such character. A project whose files hold such characters, such as `docs/User Guide.md` or `app/(dash)/[id]/page.tsx`, cannot complete those tasks inline as the call is shown. Runners then rewrite the command on their own, which the shell-commands invariant rules out. Some failures are silent: a `$name` expands, a backtick runs a command, and in bash a bracket glob can match a different existing file and commit it in place of the recorded one.

open-question.question: The recommendation pass renders the `question` and `option` attributes of `<depends-on>` and `<recommendation>` by hand, its prose naming only `&` and `<` as characters to write as entities, so a `"` in a Short Title or an alternative id yields a fragment the tool refuses as malformed XML. How is a `"` kept from breaking those attributes: by the pass's prose naming it as a character to write as an entity, by refusing it where titles and ids are created, or is the case left as it is?

recommendation.option: Leave the attributes as they are

open-question.recommendation: The tool refuses the fragment with the document unchanged and the pass's one re-send repairs it, so the failure is loud and self-correcting, and no recorded subject has ever met it.

alternative.id: Leave the attributes as they are

open-question.alternative: Nothing changes at the recommendation pass, the agent, or the tool: a `"` in a hand-rendered attribute keeps yielding a fragment the tool refuses, and the pass's existing step 6 corrects the refused block against its `Error:` line and re-sends it once. CLAUDE.md records the entry as accepted, with the reason that the refusal is never silent and is corrected by the re-send, and that no new title or id can carry a `"` wherever the creation-time refusals cover it; this is meant as never, not later. It costs nothing and changes no file the pass runs: the failure is loud rather than silent, the tool refuses with the document unchanged and the re-send already repairs it, and none of the 1,703 recorded answer and annotation subjects in this repository's history holds a `"`, so the case has not been met. A block whose re-send is refused again is skipped into the advisory and left without a pick, and the case stays open for every existing block and for every title or id the creation-time refusals do not cover, so whether the acceptance is honest depends on whether `"` is refused in new Short Titles and alternative ids and on how existing invalid titles are treated, axes the sibling questions own.

alternative.id: Entity rule at the recommendation pass

open-question.alternative: The recommendation pass's rendering sentence in step 4 of `core/skills/recommend-all-open-questions/SKILL.md` names `"` beside `&` and `<`: a literal `"` in an attribute value (the `question` and `option` attributes of `<depends-on>` and `<recommendation>`) is written `"`. Only that one site changes; the alternatives agent's rendering rule, the tool, and the batch fixed call stay as they are, and CLAUDE.md records the entry as fixed by the prose rule. A one-clause change at the one site the entry names closes the attribute position whatever the creation-time refusals end up covering, existing blocks included, with no tool contract or fixed call changed and so no new fixed-call test the goal would require; the document itself already stores every such value as `"`, so a runner copying an id from its whole read already holds the written form. Correctness still rests on the runner following prose rather than on anything mechanical, and the alternatives agent's identical rule (`core/agents/provide-alternatives-to-open-question.md`) keeps naming only `&` and `<`, so the two rendering rules diverge in wording; whether the clause ever bites depends on whether `"` is refused in new Short Titles and alternative ids, axes the sibling questions on those characters own.

alternative.id: Entity rule at both rendering sites

open-question.alternative: The same clause naming `"` as written `"` in an attribute value is added to both hand-rendering rules: the recommendation pass's step 4 and the alternatives agent's rendering rule for its `<alternative id>` attribute, so the two sentences stay worded alike. The tool and the fixed calls stay as they are, and CLAUDE.md records the entry as fixed by the prose rule at both sites. Every attribute the plugin's runners render by hand is covered by one rule in one wording, so an alternative id the agent writes with a `"` no longer costs that return its one repair, and the recommendation pass's later `option` attribute meets the same rule the id was written under. It touches the agent's rendering rule, which the sibling on markup in alternative text may also change, so the two edits must agree, and its second half is moot if the sibling on alternative id characters refuses `"` at `embed --alternatives`; it remains a prose rule a runner can miss.

`embed --recommendation` stops taking the `option` and `question` values as hand-rendered XML: it takes the recommended option and each depends-on pair as arguments (for example `--option` and a repeatable `--depends-on`), with only the rationale and applied principles read from standard input, and renders and escapes the attributes itself. The recommendation pass's batch call, its rendering step, and the tool's tests change with it, and the agent's rendering stays as it is. No runner renders an attribute value by hand any more, so a `"`, `&`, or `<` in a title or id can no longer produce a malformed fragment, closing the position structurally rather than by a rule the runner must remember. It changes the tool's contract and the batch fixed call, needs new tests and a CLAUDE.md invariant rewrite, and moves the titles and ids into double-quoted shell arguments, where `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are special, so the exposure shifts to the shell-quoting position whose handling the sibling questions on Short Title and alternative id characters own.

open-question.question: The commit tool repeats every git write that exits 128, up to 16 attempts over about four seconds, reading only the exit status and never git's message, so a failure no lock caused, such as a pathspec matching no file, is repeated to the last attempt before its error prints. Does the tool keep repeating every exit 128, or does it stop at once on one no lock caused, which needs it to read git's message text or to tell the two cases apart some other way?
open-question.recommendation: No lock is ever missed over git's wording or locale, and the cost is about four seconds before a failure that ends the call anyway, with git's own message still printed whole.
open-question.alternative: The commit tool keeps repeating every git write that exits 128 on the present schedule (16 attempts, 0.25 seconds apart), reading only the exit status and no message text. A failure no lock caused, such as `git add` of a pathspec matching no file, is still repeated to the last attempt before its `Error:` line prints. The committing invariant stays as written, and CLAUDE.md records the entry as accepted with its reason. Nothing changes in the tool, its tests, or the committing invariant, and no lock is ever missed because of git's wording, its locale, or a new lock message: the only cost is about four seconds before a failure that ends the call anyway, and git's own message still reaches the runner whole. Every non-lock 128 costs about four seconds and reports itself as "on all 16 attempts", which reads as a held lock and can send a runner to look for one; how often this happens depends on how the sibling question on committing a removed path settles, since that case is the one reproduced.

The tool keeps repeating every exit 128 without reading any message, but its one schedule constant is cut to a smaller window (for example a handful of attempts over about one second), so a non-lock failure surfaces sooner; nothing tells the two kinds of failure apart. The change is two constants and the retry test's bounds, with no message parsing and no new branch, and it shrinks the wasted wait on every non-lock failure in proportion. It narrows the window that absorbs another run's ordinary write, the reason the retry exists, below the bounds `tests/test_commit_retry.py` pins as decided, so concurrent runs (two completion runs, a sweep beside a completion run) collide more often; and a non-lock failure is still repeated and still reported as a multi-attempt failure.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads git's stderr and repeats the write only when it holds git's lock-file text (the `Unable to create '….lock': File exists` form that a held index, `HEAD`, or ref lock prints); every other exit 128 is passed on at once as one `Error:` line after its single attempt. Git is run with a fixed C locale so the message is not translated. The committing invariant's "no message text is read" is revised and the retry tests gain a non-lock 128 that fails on the first attempt. It stops exactly the failures that are not locks, whatever their cause, so a pathspec, repository, or permission failure is reported at once and honestly as one attempt, while every lock git reports in its standard form is still absorbed. The tool depends on git's message wording: a git version that rewords the lock message, or a lock failure printed in another form, is no longer retried and collides at once, the failure the retry was built to prevent; the fixed locale must cover every git write the tool runs.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads git's stderr and stops at once only when it matches a short stated list of failures no lock causes (starting with `pathspec '…' did not match any files`); every other exit 128, an unrecognized message included, is repeated on the present schedule. Git runs under a fixed C locale; the committing invariant is revised to name the list. A wording change in git or an unlisted message falls back to today's behaviour, so no lock is ever left unretried; the reproduced case and any later one found in the field stop at once. It closes only the failures someone has listed, so each new non-lock 128 still waits the full window until it is added, and the list is message-matching code the tool must keep current with git; if the sibling question on removed paths stops the pathspec case from reaching git, the list may hold nothing that occurs.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads no message text but checks git's own lock files, resolved through `git rev-parse --git-path` (the index lock, `HEAD.lock`, and the current branch's ref lock): it repeats the write while one of them exists, repeats it once more when none exists so a lock released between the failure and the probe is still absorbed, and passes on a further 128 with no lock file present after that second attempt. It tells a lock from a non-lock by the lock itself rather than by git's wording or locale, so the invariant's "no message text is read" can stand, and a non-lock failure ends after two attempts instead of sixteen. The tool gains file probes and a branch on what git keeps under its directory, a lock it does not probe (another ref, a packed-refs or config lock) is treated as a non-lock after two attempts, and the retry test must hold each probed lock file, so the mechanics grow more than a message match would.
